extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (metaphysics, moral philosophy, philosophy of religion)
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and analysis of Kant's discussion of physical and moral teleology, the moral proof of God, and the limits of theoretical Reason in the Critique of Judgment. Useful for understanding criteria Kant uses to judge the adequacy of teleological and moral arguments for theology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of Physical Teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical Teleology impels us to seek a Theology, but it cannot produce one; empirical investigation of purposive arrangements in nature cannot, by theoretical Reason alone, yield a determinate concept of a Supreme Being or prove its reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical/empirical grounds may justify positing intelligence behind purposive arrangements (physico-theology) but cannot justify adding the full set of divine perfections (omniscience, omnipotence, perfect goodness) without arbitrary supplements. Anti-pattern: using empirical observation alone to infer all attributes of a Deity or to claim a complete Theology has been established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical Reason cannot ground the Idea of Deity
rubrics_metrics.description: An Idea of a Supreme Being adequate for teleological judgement cannot be derived from the mere theoretical use of Reason; such an Idea rests in us fundamentally a priori by means of the practical use of Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not claim that success in physical cognition of the world (theoretical use) proves the reality of God. Theoretical Reason should ascribe no more properties to an object of experience than empirical data warrant. Where full divine attributes are assumed, Kant warns these are supplements originating in practical, not theoretical, Reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealism of final causes (Pantheism/Spinozism) is an explanation-away
rubrics_metrics.description: Explaining the purposive unity of nature as mere inherence in one substance (idealism) converts purposiveness into a misinterpretation of an ontological concept and thus 'explains away' the real question of the first ground of purposiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this as a doctrinal anti-pattern: treating apparent purposiveness as only a conceptual artifact (unity of inherence) rather than as signalling real teleological orientation. Kant notes this leads to pantheism or Spinozism and fails to address the genuine problem of final causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical Teleology cannot determine a final purpose or single intelligent Cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if physical Teleology shows purposive combinations in nature, it cannot (from empirical grounds alone) resolve discordances in purpose or determine whether there is one or many intelligent original beings as the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overreaching conclusions about unity of purpose or uniqueness of divine cause from observational teleology. Where empirical evidence is indifferent among hypotheses (many minds vs one supreme intelligence), theoretical Reason cannot decide sufficiently for Theology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Teleology: man (rational beings under moral laws) as the final purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: If Reason is to furnish a final purpose a priori, this final purpose can be none other than man—or every rational being—under moral laws; the moral law prescribes something as an end without any material condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant presents this as a fundamental proposition that common human Reason must accept: the moral law’s unconditional character makes rational beings uniquely fit to be thought of as the final purpose of creation. Use this when arguing for teleology grounded in moral, rather than merely physical, considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes of the Supreme Cause supplied by moral Teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: From the principle of the causality of the Original Being as related to the highest good, we must think of that Being not merely as Intelligence but as legislating supremely in a moral kingdom—all-knowing, all-mighty, all-good and just—properties presupposed in relation to the final purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral Teleology supplies the moral properties (wisdom, justice, goodness) necessary for a Deity conceived as guarantor of the highest good. Kant treats these attributions as grounded in the requirements of the moral purpose, not as empirical deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral proof of the Being of God via the highest good (summum bonum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because practical Reason demands a final purpose (the highest good: happiness harmonized with morality) and we cannot represent its realization through merely natural causality, we must assume a moral World-Cause (a God) to make the final purpose possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical (moral) form of proof: it shows that, to make coherent the striving for the highest good, one may postulate a moral Author of the world. Kant notes this can be given precise logical form but stresses its practical (not speculative) force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of the Highest Good (summum bonum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest good consists in the combination of the greatest welfare (happiness) of rational beings with the highest condition of the good in itself (morality); happiness is empirically conditioned while morality is a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims about final purposes, distinguish the two components: happiness (subject to empirical conditions) and moral worth (a priori). The practical need to harmonize them motivates the postulation of a moral World-Cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law as formal, unconditional legislator
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral law obliges absolutely without reference to any material purpose and supplies a subjective constitutive principle for the Idea of a final purpose; it determines a practical necessity to strive for the highest good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate moral law’s formal, unconditional character with empirical incentives. Kant emphasizes that moral obligation remains binding even if one were convinced there is no God; the law’s authority is independent of theological belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-equivalence of moral law’s validity and ontological necessity of God
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral proof does not assert that the existence of God is as necessary as the validity of the moral law; one can accept moral obligation without conceding theological proof. The postulation of God is a practical step to preserve the aim at the final purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to guard against the mistaken inference that moral obligation depends ontologically on God. Kant stresses the moral law’s authority survives theoretical unbelief; the assumption of God is a practical means to sustain the pursuit of the highest good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral sentiments motivate belief in a moral Intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective moral feelings—gratitude, obedience, humiliation before conscience—incline the mind to represent and desire a moral Intelligence (a Supreme Lord) as the object to whom duty and gratitude may be rendered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant offers this as an account of why humans psychologically tend to posit God on moral grounds. This is an explanatory criterion: moral disposition can ground the inclination to postulate a moral Author, though it does not constitute theoretical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of the validity of the moral proof (practical not theoretical)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral proof confers only practical (subjective/practical) reality to the Idea of a final purpose and to the assumption of a moral World-Cause; it does not satisfy the demands of theoretical (determinant) Reason for objective theoretical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat the moral proof as providing apodictic theoretical knowledge about nature; its role is to secure the objective practical reality required by moral striving. Kant distinguishes reflective practical judgement (where this proof has place) from determinant theoretical judgement.
